rw: Reading shows your rights, any fees or penalties, and your obligations before you sign. A signed contract is legally binding, so surprises found afterward are usually your responsibility.

ww.To avoid having to talk with the seller: Contracts are about legal terms, not conversation; avoiding the seller does not protect you, and reading the document is what actually prevents costly surprises later.
ww.To make the document last longer on a sh: Reading has no effect on how long paper lasts; the purpose of reviewing a contract is to learn the terms you are legally agreeing to follow.
ww.To make sure the font is easy to read on: Font readability is a minor formatting detail; the real reason to read is to learn the binding terms, costs and duties the contract places on you.

rw: High-pressure deadlines are a classic sales tactic. Slowing down lets you compare competing offers, read every term, ask questions, and walk away if the deal is not truly good.

ww.Share financial details with the seller: Sharing financial details such as account or Social Security numbers with a pushy seller increases fraud risk and does nothing to help you evaluate the deal.
ww.Sign immediately to avoid missing out on: Signing immediately because of pressure is exactly what high-pressure sellers want; you could miss hidden fees or poor terms and have little chance to reconsider.
ww.Sign without reading to save time and ef: Signing without reading means agreeing to unknown fees, penalties and obligations; a contract is binding whether or not you read it, so skipping it is risky.

rw: Federal law caps cardholder liability for unauthorized charges at $50 and lets you dispute charges while the bank investigates, so you are not out your own money.

ww.A gift card: Gift cards work like cash, so if one is lost, stolen or used by a scammer, there is generally little or no way to recover the money.
ww.Cash on delivery: Cash on delivery means paying before you can verify the goods, and there is no automatic dispute process, so recovering money from a bad seller is difficult.
ww.A wire transfer: Wire transfers are nearly instant and very hard to reverse, which is why scammers prefer them; they offer little consumer protection against unauthorized or fraudulent payments.

rw: Core consumer rights, such as those in the Consumer Bill of Rights, include safety, being informed, choice and being heard, which protect buyers from fraud and misleading claims.

ww.The right to ignore store policies if th: Store policies such as return rules apply regardless of price, and consumer rights do not let buyers ignore them; rights concern fair treatment, not exemption from rules.
ww.The right to avoid paying sales tax on p: Sales tax is a legal obligation set by state and local governments; consumer rights do not exempt buyers from it on their purchases.
ww.The right to buy anything you want for f: No law gives people free goods; consumer rights protect fair treatment and honest information in the marketplace, not a right to get products without paying.

rw: The FTC enforces laws against unfair or deceptive practices, including false advertising, and also takes consumer complaints and shuts down scams, making it the main consumer protection agency.

ww.The Internal Revenue Service (IRS): The IRS collects federal taxes and enforces the tax code; it has no primary role in policing deceptive advertising claims made to consumers.
ww.The Social Security Administration: The Social Security Administration runs retirement, disability and survivor benefit programs, not consumer protection or advertising regulation of businesses.
ww.The Federal Reserve Board system: The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy and supervises banks to keep the financial system stable; it does not regulate advertising claims aimed at consumers.

rw: Credit lets you obtain money, goods or services now and repay later, usually with interest, based on the lender's trust that you will pay as promised.

ww.Money that you receive as a gift from yo: A gift is money given freely with no repayment expected, so it is not credit, which always involves an obligation to repay the lender later.
ww.Money that you earn from a regular paych: Paycheck earnings are income you have already worked for, not borrowed funds; credit is a different concept because it creates a debt that must be repaid.
ww.Money that you deposit into a savings ac: Deposits into savings are your own money being set aside; credit is the opposite, since you use someone else's money and owe it back.

rw: A credit score, often 300 to 850 in the FICO model, summarizes your credit report to predict how likely you are to repay debts, which lenders use to decide approvals and rates.

ww.A number that shows how much money you h: Savings are shown on bank statements and are not part of a credit score, which is calculated from your borrowing and repayment behavior instead.
ww.A number that shows how many credit card: The number of cards is only a small part of the picture; a credit score measures repayment reliability, not simply how many cards you hold.
ww.A number that shows how much you earn ea: Income is not part of a credit score calculation; lenders may ask for income separately, but the score reflects your credit history only.

rw: Payment history is the largest FICO factor, about 35 percent of the score, because lenders care most about whether you pay bills on time.

ww.Your age in years: Age in years is not a factor in credit scores, and the law prohibits using age to discriminate in credit; length of credit history is different.
ww.Your favorite store: Your favorite store has no effect on your score; only reported credit behavior such as payments and balances is used in scoring models.
ww.Your zip code: Zip code is not used in credit scoring, and using location to discriminate could violate fair lending laws; the score uses credit account data.

rw: Utilization is your balances divided by your credit limits, shown as a percent. Keeping it under about 30 percent helps your score, and lower is generally better.

ww.The number of credit cards in your walle: Counting cards in your wallet is not utilization; utilization compares balances to credit limits, whereas the number of accounts is a separate smaller factor.
ww.The age of your oldest credit card accou: The age of your oldest account relates to length of credit history, a different scoring factor from utilization, which looks at how much of your limit you use.
ww.The interest rate on your credit card ba: Interest rate (APR) is the cost of borrowing and is not what utilization measures; utilization compares the balance you carry to your available limit.

rw: Utilization equals balance divided by limit: $500 / $2,000 = 0.25, or 25 percent. This is under the commonly recommended 30 percent mark for healthy credit scores.

ww.50%: 50 percent would require a $1,000 balance on a $2,000 limit; here $500 divided by $2,000 is only 0.25, so this is too high.
ww.75%: 75 percent would mean a $1,500 balance on a $2,000 limit; with a $500 balance the ratio is $500 / $2,000, which equals 25 percent, not 75.
ww.400%: 400 percent comes from dividing limit by balance ($2,000 / $500 = 4) which inverts the formula; utilization is balance divided by limit, giving 25 percent.

rw: APR, annual percentage rate, expresses the yearly cost of credit including interest and certain fees, letting you compare loans and cards on equal terms.

ww.The total balance that you owe on the ca: The balance is the amount owed right now; APR is a rate that describes the yearly cost of borrowing, not a dollar balance.
ww.The credit limit that is set on your car: The credit limit is the maximum you can borrow on the card, set by the issuer; APR is the interest rate and is unrelated to the limit.
ww.The amount of your required monthly paym: The monthly payment is a dollar amount due each billing cycle; APR is a percentage rate and does not by itself tell you the payment.

rw: Minimum payments are mostly interest, so the balance shrinks slowly, interest compounds on what remains, and repayment can stretch for years and cost far more overall.

ww.Interest stops being charged on the bala: Interest continues on any unpaid balance, so paying only the minimum does not stop it; most of a minimum payment can go toward interest.
ww.Your credit limit doubles right away wit: Paying the minimum does not raise your limit; limit increases require issuer approval and are unrelated to how little you pay each month.
ww.The balance is erased from the account i: The minimum payment covers only a small part of the balance, so most of the debt remains and is not erased after one payment.

rw: If you pay your statement balance in full by the due date, usually about 21 or more days after the cycle ends, you pay no interest on purchases.

ww.Time when the debt is forgiven by the le: A grace period does not forgive debt; the lender still expects full repayment, and it only gives you time before interest starts on new purchases.
ww.Time during which the card cannot be use: Cards remain usable during a grace period; it refers to interest-free time on purchases, not any suspension of the card's use.
ww.Time when you owe double the normal inte: A grace period never doubles interest; penalty rates are a separate consequence of late payments, while a grace period is a benefit that avoids interest.

rw: A secured card requires a refundable cash deposit that usually becomes your credit limit, so the issuer is protected, and it helps people build or rebuild credit.

ww.A card that comes with no spending limit: Every card has a limit; a secured card's limit is typically tied to the deposit, and no card gives truly unlimited spending.
ww.A card whose balance never needs to be r: Balances on secured cards must be repaid like any card; if you do not pay, the issuer can keep your deposit and you still owe interest.
ww.A card that is issued only to businesses: Secured cards are mainly offered to individual consumers with limited or damaged credit, not restricted to businesses.

rw: Collateral, such as a car or home, secures the lender, who can repossess or foreclose if you default. That lower risk usually means lower interest rates.

ww.A loan guaranteed by the borrower's sign: A loan with only a signature and no property backing is unsecured; a secured loan specifically involves pledged collateral such as a car or house.
ww.A loan from a friend that has no written: A secured loan involves property pledged as collateral; informal loans with no paperwork have no collateral or legal protections and are not the definition.
ww.A loan that carries no repayment require: All loans carry a repayment requirement; a secured loan is defined by collateral that the lender can claim if repayment fails, not by lack of repayment.

rw: An unsecured loan, such as a personal loan or credit card, has no collateral, so approval and rates depend on your credit score and income.

ww.A loan that is backed by a car or a truc: A loan backed by a car or truck is a secured loan, since the vehicle is collateral the lender can repossess if you default.
ww.A loan from a pawn shop that holds an it: Pawn loans are secured by the item you leave, so the pawn shop holds collateral; that makes them secured rather than unsecured.
ww.A loan that is backed by a house or a fl: A loan backed by a house or flat is a mortgage, a secured loan where the property is collateral the lender can foreclose on.

rw: A cosigner signs the loan alongside the borrower and becomes legally liable for repayment if the borrower defaults. This can help a borrower with thin credit qualify.

ww.A person who gives the borrower extra mo: A cosigner does not give the borrower spending money; they pledge their own credit and take legal responsibility for the debt if the borrower does not pay.
ww.A person who approves the loan paperwork: Approving paperwork is the lender's job; a cosigner is a third party who guarantees repayment, not an employee of the bank.
ww.A person who inspects collateral for the: Inspecting or appraising collateral is done by an appraiser or lender; a cosigner's role is to guarantee repayment with their own credit.

rw: The loan term, such as 36 months or 30 years, is the repayment period. Longer terms lower monthly payments but usually raise total interest paid.

ww.The interest rate that is charged on the: The interest rate is the cost of borrowing as a percentage; the term is a separate feature that states how long you have to repay.
ww.The amount of money that was first borro: The amount first borrowed is the principal; the term describes the repayment period, not the loan size.
ww.The fee that is charged for a late payme: A late fee is a penalty charged for missing a due date; the term is simply the length of the repayment period.

rw: Spreading $10,000 over 60 payments rather than 36 makes each payment smaller, but interest accrues longer, so total interest is higher on the 5-year loan.

ww.The 3-year loan, with lower total intere: The 3-year loan has the higher monthly payment because the same principal is paid off in fewer payments; it saves total interest but costs more each month.
ww.Both have exactly the same monthly payme: Payments depend on the term: 36 payments are larger than 60 payments for the same principal and rate, so they cannot be exactly equal.
ww.Neither one has any payment due at all e: Any loan with a balance requires regular payments until it is repaid; neither term avoids payments, so this option makes no sense.

rw: Principal is the original amount borrowed or invested, which interest is calculated on. Payments reduce the principal balance over time, lowering future interest.

ww.The extra amount charged for it: The extra amount charged for borrowing is interest, not principal; principal is the original sum before interest is added.
ww.The monthly payment amount: The monthly payment typically combines principal and interest; it is not the same thing as principal, which is only the amount borrowed.
ww.The fee for paying very late: A fee for paying late is a penalty charge; it is separate from the principal, which is the original amount borrowed.

rw: Simple interest = P x r x t = $2,000 x 0.06 x 2 = $240. Interest is figured only on the original principal, so it does not compound.

ww.$24: $24 would be interest on only a small base; simple interest is principal times rate times time, which is $2,000 x 0.06 x 2, not $24.
ww.$120: $120 is just one year of interest ($2,000 x 0.06); the loan runs two years, so the interest must be doubled to $240.
ww.$2,240: $2,240 is the total owed at the end (principal $2,000 plus $240 interest), not the interest itself, which is $240.

rw: A credit report lists your accounts, balances, payment history, inquiries and public records, which lenders use to judge how reliably you borrow and repay.

ww.Your shopping lists and receipts: Shopping lists and receipts are not tracked by credit bureaus; the report records credit accounts and payment behavior only.
ww.Your bank passwords and card numbers: Credit reports do not show your passwords, and card numbers are truncated; keeping them off the report protects your private information.
ww.Your medical history and records: Medical history is private and not part of a credit report, though unpaid medical debts sent to collections can sometimes appear as accounts.

rw: Under federal law you may get a free report from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion at least once every 12 months at AnnualCreditReport.com, helping you catch errors early.

ww.Only after two denials: Free reports are not limited to people who have been denied credit, although a denial also gives you an additional free report.
ww.Never once in a year: Federal law allows free reports, and weekly access has been offered through AnnualCreditReport.com, so saying never is wrong.
ww.Once every ten years: Reports are available far more often than every ten years; that interval would make it hard to catch errors or identity theft.

rw: The Fair Credit Reporting Act lets you dispute inaccurate items; the bureau must investigate, normally within 30 days, and correct or delete wrong information. Include documents as proof.

ww.Close all your accounts right away to be: Closing accounts does not remove an error and can lower your score by cutting available credit and shortening your history; the mistake still needs fixing.
ww.Ignore it because errors fix themselves: Errors do not fix themselves, and they may hurt loan approvals or rates meanwhile, so waiting leaves the problem unresolved.
ww.Pay the debt even if it is not yours to: Paying a debt that is not yours could be mistaken for accepting responsibility; the correct step is disputing the error, not paying it.

rw: Identity theft is the unauthorized use of someone's personal data, such as a Social Security number, to open accounts or commit fraud. Monitoring reports and freezing credit help prevent it.

ww.Sharing a photo online with a close frie: Sharing a photo with a friend is normal sharing with consent, not stealing someone's identity or using it for fraud.
ww.Forgetting your password to an online ac: Forgetting your own password is an access problem and not a crime; identity theft requires another person misusing your identifying information.
ww.Changing your own name through a court p: Legally changing your own name through a court is a lawful personal choice, unlike identity theft, which is the misuse of another person's data.

rw: A credit freeze restricts access to your report so lenders cannot check it, making it hard for thieves to open new accounts in your name. It is free to place and lift.

ww.Raises your credit score by a set number: A freeze does not change your score; it only restricts access to your report, so it cannot add points to your credit score.
ww.Cancels all of the cards that you hold t: A freeze does not close accounts; your existing cards stay open and usable, since it only affects new credit inquiries.
ww.Erases all of the debts that you owe to: A freeze erases nothing; your debts and history remain, and you still owe everything you borrowed.

rw: A payday loan is a small, short-term loan, usually due on the borrower's next payday, with very high fees equivalent to APRs of 400 percent or more.

ww.A long-term low-cost loan from a credit: Credit unions offer low-cost loans such as payday alternative loans, but a payday loan is the opposite: short-term, high cost, and typically due within weeks.
ww.A grant that never needs any repayment a: Payday loans always must be repaid, usually with a large fee; grants and scholarships are the money that does not require repayment.
ww.A loan with no fees and no interest char: Payday loans carry high fees and effective interest rates, often $15 per $100 borrowed for two weeks, so claiming no cost is false.

rw: Fees equivalent to triple-digit APRs, plus short due dates, push borrowers to roll over or borrow again, making debt grow instead of shrinking.

ww.They offer some of the lowest rates for: Payday loans have some of the highest rates, often 400 percent APR or more, not the lowest, which is why they are considered risky.
ww.They are insured by the federal governme: Payday lenders are not government-insured, and borrowers have no guarantee of protection; their high costs are the main danger.
ww.They are slowly repaid over thirty years: Payday loans are due in weeks, not decades, and carry high rates; a thirty-year low-rate loan describes something like a mortgage.

rw: Debt consolidation merges several debts into one loan or payment, often at a lower rate, which simplifies repayment and may cut interest costs if the terms are better.

ww.Ignoring the debts until they somehow va: Ignoring debts does not make them vanish; interest, late fees and collections can grow, and missed payments harm your credit score.
ww.Splitting one large debt into many small: Consolidation combines debts rather than splitting them; splitting one debt into many pieces would make them harder to manage, not simpler.
ww.Borrowing more money so you can spend fr: Taking on more borrowing for spending increases debt; consolidation is about organizing and paying off existing debts, ideally at a lower rate.

rw: The avalanche method pays minimums on all debts and puts extra money toward the highest interest rate first, minimizing total interest paid over time.

ww.The snowball method: The snowball method pays off the smallest balance first for motivation, so it does not focus on the highest interest rate and may cost more.
ww.The random method: Paying in a random order has no strategy behind it and does not target high rates, so it is not a recognized money-saving method.
ww.The minimum-only method: Paying only the minimums keeps debts alive longest and builds the most interest; it is not a method for targeting high-rate debt.

rw: Bankruptcy, such as Chapter 7 or Chapter 13, is a federal court process that can discharge or restructure debts but stays on credit reports for 7 to 10 years.

ww.A program that pays out tax refunds each: Tax refunds are paid by the government after you file a return; bankruptcy is a court process dealing with debts, not an income payment program.
ww.A type of savings plan for families and: Savings plans such as 529s help families save for college; bankruptcy is a legal debt relief process, not a saving option.
ww.A way to make sure you never owe any len: Bankruptcy does not guarantee you will never borrow again; it damages credit for years, and you can still take on new debt afterward.

rw: A mortgage is a loan used to buy property where the home is the collateral, so the lender can foreclose if payments stop. Terms often last 15 or 30 years.

ww.A loan that has no collateral behind it: A loan with no collateral is unsecured; a mortgage is the opposite, because the real estate itself serves as collateral for the loan.
ww.A loan that is taken out to pay for scho: A loan for education is a student loan; a mortgage specifically finances the purchase of property.
ww.A loan that is taken out to buy a car: Auto loans finance vehicles; a mortgage is a loan used to buy real estate, with the property as collateral.

rw: A down payment is cash paid upfront, which lowers the loan amount, reduces interest costs and may help avoid private mortgage insurance on home loans.

ww.Increases the interest rate on the whole: A bigger down payment generally lowers, not raises, the interest paid, since you borrow less; it does not increase the rate on the whole loan.
ww.Adds fees to the loan for the whole term: A down payment does not add fees to the loan; it reduces the amount financed, so total interest and monthly payments usually fall.
ww.Eliminates the need for a loan always an: A down payment cuts what you borrow but rarely removes the loan entirely, since it is only part of the price of a large purchase.

rw: Amount financed equals price minus down payment: $20,000 - $4,000 = $16,000. A larger down payment means a smaller loan and less interest.

ww.$24,000: $24,000 adds the down payment to the price instead of subtracting it; a down payment reduces the amount financed.
ww.$4,000: $4,000 is the down payment itself, not the amount financed; the loan covers the remaining price after the down payment.
ww.$20,000: $20,000 is the full price, which would be financed only if nothing were paid down; with $4,000 down, less is borrowed.

rw: A student loan is borrowed money for education costs that must be repaid with interest. Federal loans often have lower rates and more protections than private loans.

ww.A grant that never needs to be repaid by: Student loans must be repaid, usually with interest; money that does not need repayment is a grant, so this option describes a different thing.
ww.A scholarship that a school awards to a: Scholarships are awards that need no repayment; a student loan is borrowed money with repayment and interest.
ww.A free gift of money from the federal go: Student loans are borrowed and must be repaid; a free gift from the government would be a grant, such as the Pell Grant.

rw: Grants and scholarships never need repayment, and federal aid usually has lower rates and flexible repayment, so they should come before private borrowing. Start by filing the FAFSA.

ww.Private loans from big banks first of al: Private bank loans usually have fewer protections and often higher rates, so they should come after free aid and federal loans.
ww.Credit cards with high interest from a b: High-interest credit cards are an expensive way to pay tuition because balances grow quickly with interest, so they are a poor first choice.
ww.Payday loans from short-term lenders fir: Payday loans have extremely high fees and short terms, making them a costly and risky way to pay for college.

rw: A late fee is a penalty charged when a payment arrives after its due date. Late payments can also hurt your credit score if they are over 30 days past due.

ww.A tax that is charged on interest earned: Taxes on interest earned are a tax matter; a late fee is a penalty for paying a bill late.
ww.A reward that is given for paying early: A reward for paying early is a discount or incentive; a late fee is the opposite, a penalty for paying after the due date.
ww.A service that the bank gives to every c: A late fee is a penalty rather than a bank service, and customers can avoid it by paying on time.

rw: On-time payments and low balances are the biggest drivers of a score, since payment history and utilization together make up well over half of it.

ww.Miss payments now and then to save cash: Missed payments are reported to the bureaus and can drop your score significantly, so skipping them harms your credit history rather than helping it.
ww.Close every account that you have open: Closing accounts reduces available credit, raising utilization and shortening history, which can lower your score rather than build it.
ww.Max out your cards every single month: Maxing out cards creates very high utilization, which lowers scores and signals risk to lenders; keeping balances low builds good credit.

rw: A hard inquiry occurs when a lender checks your credit because you applied for credit. It can lower your score slightly for about a year and stays on your report for two years.

ww.A question from a cashier at the till: A cashier's question has no connection to credit; a hard inquiry is a lender looking at your credit report after you apply.
ww.A bank statement mailed to your home: A mailed bank statement is a regular account summary and does not count as an inquiry on your credit report.
ww.A check you make on your own report: Checking your own report is a soft inquiry, which does not affect your score, unlike a hard inquiry from a lender.

rw: Predatory lending uses deception, hidden fees, or excessive rates to exploit borrowers, often targeting people with low incomes or little financial knowledge. Warning signs include pressure and unclear terms.

ww.Lending only to people who have great cr: Lending only to people with strong credit is standard prime lending, not predatory; predatory lending targets vulnerable borrowers with unfair terms.
ww.Lending money with clear and fair terms: Clear and fair terms for everyone describes responsible lending; predatory lending uses hidden or deceptive terms instead.
ww.Lending money at the lowest market rate: Lending at the lowest market rate is fair pricing, not predatory; predatory lenders charge high or hidden costs to exploit borrowers.

rw: A premium is the regular payment, often monthly or yearly, that you make to keep insurance coverage active, and it is the price of the policy.

ww.The amount you pay before the coverage s: What you pay before coverage begins is the deductible, not the premium; the premium is what you pay to hold the policy.
ww.The amount the insurer pays after a loss: The amount the insurer pays after a loss is the claim payout, not the premium, which is what you pay in.
ww.The maximum coverage that you can claim: The maximum coverage is the policy limit, the most the insurer will pay; the premium is the price of the policy.

rw: A deductible is the amount you pay out of pocket on a covered loss before insurance pays the rest. Higher deductibles usually mean lower premiums.

ww.The profit that the insurer makes each y: Insurer profit is its own business result; a deductible is the portion of a covered loss you pay yourself first.
ww.The premium that you pay each year in fu: The premium is the regular price of the policy; the deductible is a separate out-of-pocket amount paid when you file a claim.
ww.The coverage limit that is set in the po: The coverage limit is the maximum the insurer pays; the deductible is the amount you pay first, so they are different parts of a policy.

rw: Insurer pays the bill minus the deductible: $1,800 - $500 = $1,300. Alex pays the first $500 and the insurer covers the remaining covered amount.

ww.$1,800: $1,800 is the full bill and ignores the deductible; the insurer only pays what remains after Alex covers the first $500.
ww.$500: $500 is the deductible, which is what Alex pays, not the insurer; the insurer pays the remaining $1,300.
ww.$2,300: $2,300 adds the deductible to the bill instead of subtracting it; the insurer cannot pay more than the covered bill, which is $1,800 minus $500.

rw: Liability insurance pays for injuries or property damage you cause to others and covers legal defense costs, up to your policy limits, protecting your assets from lawsuits.

ww.Your own medical bills and nothing else: Your own medical bills are covered by health or medical payments coverage; liability insurance pays for harm you cause to others.
ww.Damage to your own property and nothing: Damage to your own property is covered by collision, comprehensive or property coverage; liability pays for others' losses.
ww.Routine maintenance and repairs on your: Routine maintenance is not insurable because it is a predictable expense, and liability coverage pays for harm to others, not upkeep.

rw: Collision coverage pays to repair or replace your own car after a crash with another vehicle or object, regardless of who was at fault, minus your deductible.

ww.Oil changes and other routine upkeep for: Oil changes are routine maintenance costs, which are predictable and not covered by any car insurance; collision pays for accident damage.
ww.Theft of the car and nothing else beside: Theft is covered by comprehensive coverage rather than collision, which pays for damage from hitting something or being hit.
ww.Damage to other people's cars only, not: Damage to other people's cars is covered by liability coverage; collision pays to repair your own car.

rw: Comprehensive covers damage not caused by a collision, such as theft, fire, vandalism, falling objects, floods and hail, usually minus your deductible.

ww.Tire wear from normal driving on public: Normal tire wear is routine maintenance and not an insured event; comprehensive covers sudden, non-collision losses.
ww.Injuries to other drivers in a crash tha: Injuries to other drivers that you cause are covered by liability coverage, not comprehensive, which covers your own vehicle.
ww.Damage from a crash that you cause yours: Crash damage you cause is covered by collision coverage on your own car, whereas comprehensive covers non-collision events.

rw: Renters insurance covers your belongings and your liability if you cause harm, but the building belongs to the landlord, who insures it separately.

ww.Unpaid rent owed to the landlord by the: Renters insurance does not pay unpaid rent; rent is a contractual obligation between tenant and landlord that insurance does not cover.
ww.The building structure that the landlord: The landlord insures the building structure with their own property policy; renters insurance covers the tenant's contents and liability.
ww.The income that the landlord earns from: A landlord's rental income is protected by the landlord's own policy, not by a tenant's renters insurance.

rw: Insurers price using claims statistics, and drivers under about 25 have more accidents per mile because of inexperience, so they pay higher premiums.

ww.Young drivers always own pricier cars th: Premiums are based on risk, not on vehicle price alone, and many young drivers drive older, cheaper cars.
ww.Young drivers are exempt from needing an: Young drivers are not exempt from insurance; state laws require liability coverage for almost every driver.
ww.Insurers simply dislike young people as: Insurers price using data on risk, not personal dislike; age is a measurable factor tied to accident rates.

rw: Insurers reward low-risk drivers with discounts, and choosing a higher deductible means you carry more risk yourself, which lowers your premium.

ww.Lowering the deductible all the way down: Lowering the deductible raises the premium because the insurer takes on more cost per claim, so this raises, not lowers, premiums.
ww.Driving around without any insurance cov: Driving uninsured is illegal in nearly every state and brings fines, and it does not lower premiums; it risks big personal costs.
ww.Getting several speeding tickets each ye: Speeding tickets signal risk and raise premiums, so collecting them would increase your costs, not lower them.

rw: Health insurance pays a share of medical costs for covered services such as doctor visits, hospital stays and prescriptions, protecting you from large bills. You still pay premiums and cost sharing.

ww.A loan that is used to pay hospital bill: Health insurance is not a loan; it is a contract where you pay premiums and the insurer pays covered medical costs, with no repayment of claims.
ww.A discount on memberships at local gyms: Gym discounts are a perk, not health insurance, which covers medical care such as doctor visits and hospital stays.
ww.A savings plan employers set up to help: Employer retirement savings plans like a 401(k) are about retirement, not medical care; health insurance covers medical expenses.

rw: A copay is a set dollar amount, such as $25 for a doctor visit, that you pay when you receive a covered service, separate from the premium.

ww.The yearly premium you pay to the insure: The yearly cost of the policy is the premium; a copay is a small fixed fee paid at the time of care.
ww.The total claim amount for the whole yea: A claim total for the year is not a copay; a copay is a fixed payment made per service.
ww.A fine for missing a doctor visit withou: A fine for a missed appointment is a no-show fee, and a copay is paid for covered care you actually receive.

rw: After you meet your deductible, coinsurance splits remaining costs, such as the plan paying 80 percent and you paying 20 percent, until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum.

ww.A flat fee that you pay at every single: A flat fee per visit is a copay; coinsurance is a percentage of the cost rather than a fixed amount.
ww.A penalty for using out-of-network care: Out-of-network penalties or higher costs are a separate matter; coinsurance is the percentage split of covered costs after the deductible.
ww.The monthly premium that you pay to the: The monthly premium is a fixed charge to keep the policy; coinsurance is a share of covered costs that applies when you use care.

rw: Life insurance pays a death benefit to named beneficiaries when the insured person dies, replacing lost income and covering debts, funeral costs and other expenses. Term and whole life are two common types.

ww.Coverage that pays you money when you re: Retirement income comes from pensions, annuities or savings; life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries when the insured dies.
ww.Coverage that pays for car damage and re: Car damage and repairs are covered by auto insurance, not by life insurance, which pays out upon the insured person's death.
ww.Coverage that pays for medical costs and: Medical costs and drugs are covered by health insurance, whereas life insurance pays a benefit after the insured dies.

rw: Life insurance is most useful for people with dependents such as a spouse or children who would suffer financially if that income were lost.

ww.Everyone with no dependents or debts to: People with no dependents or debts generally have little need for it, since there is no one financially relying on their income.
ww.Only people who never work at any job: People who do not work may still have family responsibilities, and this option is clearly too narrow to be a real guideline.
ww.No one at all, ever, in any situation: Life insurance is useful for those with dependents or debts, so saying no one needs it ever is false.

rw: Disability insurance replaces a portion of your income, often 60 percent, if illness or injury keeps you from working. It protects your paycheck, which is usually your largest asset.

ww.Coverage that pays for damage to a car's: Car body damage is covered by auto collision coverage, whereas disability insurance replaces income lost when injury or illness prevents work.
ww.Coverage that pays for a vacation trip a: Vacations are not covered by disability insurance; travel insurance may cover trip problems, but disability pays income when you cannot work.
ww.Coverage that pays the taxes you owe eac: Taxes are not paid by disability insurance; it replaces lost wages when you cannot work.

rw: Homeowners insurance usually covers the dwelling, personal belongings, liability for injuries on your property, and additional living expenses after a covered loss.

ww.Coverage for car accidents and repairs o: Car accidents and repairs are covered by auto insurance, a separate policy; homeowners insurance protects your house and property.
ww.Coverage that is meant for renters only: Renters insurance is for tenants; homeowners insurance covers people who own their home, and mortgage lenders often require it.
ww.Coverage that pays your mortgage if jobl: Homeowners insurance does not pay your mortgage if you lose your job; that would require special payment protection, whereas homeowners covers property damage and liability.

rw: Risk avoidance means not doing the risky activity at all, such as not driving, which removes the chance of loss completely but also gives up the benefits.

ww.Taking safety steps to lower the chance: Safety steps that lower the chance of loss are risk reduction, which accepts the activity while making it safer, not avoidance.
ww.Saving money to cover a loss that may oc: Saving money to cover a possible loss is risk retention, because you plan to absorb the cost yourself rather than avoid it.
ww.Buying insurance for a loss that may occ: Buying insurance is risk transfer, shifting the cost of a possible loss to an insurer instead of avoiding the activity.

rw: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a possible loss to another party, most commonly by buying insurance and paying premiums.

ww.Accepting a risk and paying for a loss y: Accepting a risk and paying for losses yourself is risk retention, the opposite of transferring the risk to someone else.
ww.Avoiding a risk entirely by not taking p: Avoiding a risk entirely by not taking part is risk avoidance, not transfer, because no one else takes on the loss.
ww.Reducing the chance that a loss will hap: Lowering the chance a loss happens is risk reduction, such as installing alarms; transfer moves the cost to someone else.

rw: Risk retention means accepting the risk and paying for any loss yourself, often through savings or a high deductible, and works best for small, affordable losses.

ww.Buying insurance to cover a possible los: Buying insurance to cover a possible loss is risk transfer, because the insurer takes on the cost rather than you.
ww.Installing safety devices to lower the c: Installing safety devices is risk reduction because it lowers the chance of loss, but you still bear any loss that occurs.
ww.Avoiding the risky activity altogether a: Avoiding the risky activity altogether is risk avoidance, which eliminates the exposure rather than accepting and paying for it.

rw: Smoke detectors and extinguishers lower the chance and size of a fire loss, which is risk reduction, also called loss control or prevention.

ww.Risk transfer: Risk transfer would be buying insurance or otherwise shifting the cost to another party; safety equipment does not do that.
ww.Risk retention: Risk retention means accepting the possible loss and paying yourself, whereas installing safety equipment actively tries to prevent the loss.
ww.Risk avoidance: Risk avoidance would mean not having the exposure at all, such as not owning a home; the family keeps the exposure but reduces it.

rw: A claim is a formal request to your insurer for payment after a covered loss, such as an accident or theft. The insurer investigates and pays according to policy terms, minus your deductible.

ww.A type of savings that earns monthly int: A savings type that earns interest is an account; an insurance claim is a request to the insurer for payment of a covered loss.
ww.A fee that you pay for a policy each mon: The regular fee you pay for a policy is the premium, whereas a claim is something you file after a loss.
ww.A refund of the premium you paid earlier: A refund of premiums is not a claim; a claim asks the insurer to pay for a covered loss.

rw: An exclusion lists causes, property or situations the policy will not pay for, such as floods or earthquakes under standard homeowners policies. Reading exclusions helps you spot gaps in coverage.

ww.A discount for very good driving habits: A discount for good driving is a credit that lowers cost; an exclusion limits what the policy pays.
ww.The monthly cost of the whole policy: The monthly cost of the policy is the premium; an exclusion is a specific loss or situation the policy does not cover.
ww.The coverage limit in the policy: The coverage limit is the most the insurer will pay; an exclusion is something not covered at all.

rw: Standard homeowners policies exclude flood damage, so owners must buy separate flood insurance, often through the National Flood Insurance Program. Check exclusions before disasters strike.

ww.The owner is not allowed to file any cla: Owners are allowed to file claims on any policy; the issue is that flood damage is not a covered cause of loss in a standard policy.
ww.The insurer simply made a mistake in the: The insurer did not err; the policy terms exclude floods, and the written exclusion is the reason the claim is denied.
ww.Floods are always covered in standard po: Floods are generally excluded from standard homeowners policies, and flood coverage costs extra, so this option states the opposite of the truth.

rw: An emergency fund covers unexpected costs such as car repairs or lost income, so you avoid high-interest debt. Experts recommend three to six months of expenses.

ww.It is meant only for paying for vacation: An emergency fund is meant for unexpected needs such as job loss or repairs, not planned expenses like vacations.
ww.It replaces the need for all your insura: An emergency fund handles smaller shocks, but it cannot replace insurance, because large losses like a house fire or major illness can far exceed savings.
ww.It increases the amount of risk a family: An emergency fund reduces a family's exposure to financial risk by providing a cushion, so it does not increase risk.

rw: Insurers set prices differently using their own formulas, so the same coverage can cost very different amounts, and shopping around can save significant money.

ww.It removes the need for coverage: Comparing quotes does not remove the need for coverage; it helps you choose among policies, not skip insurance.
ww.It guarantees the lowest rate: Comparing quotes can find a lower price, but it cannot guarantee that you get the lowest rate available anywhere, as rates change.
ww.All companies charge the same: Companies price risk differently, which is exactly why comparing quotes is worth doing; rates are not identical across insurers.

rw: Investing means buying assets such as stocks, bonds or real estate expecting them to grow in value or earn income over time, though returns are not guaranteed.

ww.Borrowing money just to have fun: Borrowing for fun is spending financed by debt, not investing, which aims to build value over time through assets.
ww.Hiding cash in a drawer at home daily: Hiding cash in a drawer earns nothing and loses value to inflation; investing puts money to work in assets.
ww.Spending money on daily needs each month: Spending on daily needs is consumption, not investing, because it does not aim to grow your money.

rw: A stock represents a share of ownership in a corporation, so shareholders may gain from price growth and dividends and often can vote on company matters.

ww.A deposit held at a local bank: A deposit at a bank is a savings or checking account, not a stock; stocks represent ownership in a company.
ww.A type of insurance policy for cars: Car insurance is a protection product; a stock is an ownership share in a company, so they are different things.
ww.A loan made to a company and repaid: A loan to a company repaid with interest describes a bond; a stock gives ownership rather than lending.

rw: A mutual fund pools money from many investors to buy a diversified mix of stocks, bonds or other securities, managed by professionals, giving small investors instant diversification.

ww.A savings account at a local bank branch: A bank savings account is an insured deposit; a mutual fund pools many investors' money into securities and is not a bank deposit.
ww.A loan that a bank makes to a single bor: A bank loan to one borrower is lending; a mutual fund pools money from many investors rather than lending to a single borrower.
ww.A single stock owned by one person alone: A mutual fund spreads money across many holdings, so it is not a single stock owned by one person alone.

rw: An index fund tracks a market index such as the S&P 500, so it holds the same stocks. It typically has low fees and broad diversification.

ww.A fund guaranteed to never lose any of y: No investment is guaranteed against loss; an index fund can lose value whenever the market it tracks declines.
ww.A fund that tries to beat the market thr: Trying to beat the market describes an actively managed fund; an index fund simply tracks an index with low trading.
ww.A fund that holds only one stock at a ti: An index fund holds many securities in its index, which makes it diversified rather than a single stock holding.

rw: Diversification spreads money across different assets, industries or regions so a loss in one has less effect on the whole, lowering risk without necessarily lowering returns.

ww.Borrowing money in order to invest it in: Borrowing to invest is leverage, which increases risk, whereas diversification reduces risk by spreading investments.
ww.Putting all your money in one single sto: Putting everything in one stock is the opposite of diversifying and leaves you fully exposed to that company's performance.
ww.Holding only cash and nothing else at al: Holding only cash is a single asset type and gives up growth; diversification means owning a range of different investments.

rw: Higher expected returns generally come with higher risk, as seen with stocks versus savings accounts. Investors need to be paid for accepting the chance of loss.

ww.Risk and return are unrelated, so one te: Risk and return are linked, because investors demand higher potential returns for taking on greater uncertainty; saying they are unrelated is wrong.
ww.Higher returns always come with no risk: Higher returns do not come without risk; stocks may earn more over time but can fall sharply in the short term.
ww.Low risk always guarantees high returns: Low-risk investments such as savings accounts and Treasury bills usually pay low returns, so low risk never guarantees high returns.

rw: A single start-up stock can lose all its value, and its price is volatile, so it carries high risk, though it also has potential for large gains.

ww.A broad index fund of many stocks: A broad index fund holds many stocks and is diversified, so it is far less risky than one company's shares.
ww.A federally insured savings account: Federally insured savings accounts are protected up to $250,000 by the FDIC, making them one of the safest options.
ww.A U.S. Treasury bill held to the end: Treasury bills are backed by the U.S. government and, held to maturity, return the principal, making them very low risk.

rw: A dividend is a payment to shareholders from company profits, often quarterly, which gives investors income in addition to any price growth.

ww.A fee that is paid to a broker each time: Broker fees are commissions or charges for trades, not dividends, which are money received by owners.
ww.Interest that is charged to each borrowe: Interest charged to borrowers is a cost of loans; a dividend is a payment to stock owners, not a charge.
ww.A tax that is charged on stock trades: Taxes on trades are a government charge, while a dividend is money that a company pays to its shareholders.

rw: A capital gain is the profit when you sell an asset, such as a stock, for more than you paid. Assets held over a year get lower long-term tax rates.

ww.Wages that are earned from a job each mo: Wages earned from a job are ordinary income, not capital gains, which come from selling assets for more than their cost.
ww.A gift of money from a relative in the f: Gifts from relatives are not capital gains; a gain arises only from the sale of an asset at a profit.
ww.Interest that is paid on a savings accou: Interest on savings is interest income and is taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains, which arise from selling assets.

rw: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored plan where employees contribute from their paychecks, often pre-tax, and employers may match contributions. Investments grow tax-deferred until retirement.

ww.A car loan from a local bank for a new c: A car loan is borrowing to buy a vehicle; a 401(k) is a retirement account, named after a section of the tax code.
ww.A type of health insurance plan for work: Health insurance plans cover medical costs; a 401(k) is a retirement savings plan, so these are different products.
ww.A savings plan that is meant for college: Savings for college costs is described by a 529 plan, whereas a 401(k) is for retirement.

rw: Employer matches 100 percent of contributions up to 3 percent of pay: 3% x $30,000 = $900 from you, so the employer adds an equal $900.

ww.$90: $90 comes from misplacing the decimal; 3 percent of $30,000 is $900, so the match equals $900 rather than $90.
ww.$300: $300 is only 1 percent of $30,000; the match is 100 percent of your 3 percent, which is $900.
ww.$9,000: $9,000 would be 30 percent of pay; 3 percent of $30,000 equals $900, so the match is $900.

rw: An IRA, or individual retirement arrangement, is a personal account for retirement savings that offers tax advantages, such as deductions or tax-free growth. Annual limits apply.

ww.A loan that is made to retired people on: An IRA is an account, not a loan, and retirees are not its only users; people save in one while still working.
ww.An insurance policy for retirees only: An IRA is an investment account and not an insurance policy; anyone with earned income can contribute, not just retirees.
ww.A government tax form filed by retirees: An IRA is a retirement account, not a tax form for retirees; anyone with earned income can contribute.

rw: Roth IRA contributions come from after-tax money, so qualified withdrawals in retirement, including earnings, are tax-free. This helps if you expect higher taxes later.

ww.It pays a guaranteed return of ten perce: No retirement account guarantees a return; Roth IRA investments rise and fall with the market, and no fixed ten percent is promised.
ww.Contributions are tax-deductible and wit: That describes a traditional IRA, where contributions may be deductible and withdrawals are taxed; a Roth works the opposite way.
ww.Withdrawals are always free of any rules: Roth withdrawals follow rules, such as the age 59 and a half and five-year requirements for tax-free earnings, so they are not rule-free.

rw: Compounding means earnings generate their own earnings, so more years lets small deposits grow substantially. Starting at 25 instead of 35 can mean much more by retirement.

ww.Fees are lower for all of the early inve: Fees are charged by funds and brokers regardless of how early you start, so starting early does not lower fees.
ww.Taxes disappear for early investors in e: Taxes still apply to investors of any age, so starting early does not remove them; the benefit is growth over time.
ww.Early investors never lose any money at: Early investors can still lose money, as markets fluctuate; time horizon helps by allowing recovery, but nothing guarantees gains.

rw: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a set amount at regular intervals, such as $200 monthly, so you buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when high.

ww.Waiting for the lowest price to appear a: Waiting for the lowest price is market timing, which is very hard to do and not what dollar-cost averaging involves.
ww.Selling when prices fall by a fair amoun: Selling after prices fall is a reaction to losses and not dollar-cost averaging, which involves steady, regular buying.
ww.Investing everything at once on a hunch: Investing everything at once on a hunch is lump-sum investing based on guessing, not the regular steady purchases of dollar-cost averaging.

rw: A brokerage account lets you buy and sell investments such as stocks, bonds and funds through a brokerage firm. Unlike retirement accounts, it has no special tax benefits.

ww.An account that guarantees a set rate of: No account guarantees a rate of return; a brokerage account holds investments whose value rises and falls.
ww.An account that is used only for borrowi: Borrowing is done through loans or credit lines; a brokerage account is for investing, though margin accounts can borrow.
ww.An account that is used for paying bills: Paying bills is the job of a checking account; a brokerage account is used to hold and trade investments.

rw: Fees come out of your balance, so less money stays invested to compound. Even a 1 percent difference in annual fees can cost tens of thousands over decades.

ww.Fees only affect investors who hold for: Fees affect all long-term investors, and the effect grows with time, so they are not limited to short-term holders.
ww.Fees actually increase returns over time: Fees subtract from your returns and never add to them, so claiming they increase returns is incorrect.
ww.Fees have no effect at all on returns ov: Fees compound against you over decades, so even small percentages matter, meaning they do have an effect on long-term returns.

rw: A time horizon is how long you expect to keep money invested before you need it. Longer horizons can handle more stock risk, while short ones favor safer assets.

ww.The time it takes to open an account: Opening an account is a quick setup task; a time horizon is the length of time you plan to invest before needing the money.
ww.The date a company was first founded: The founding date of a company is unrelated to your own investing plans; time horizon refers to how long you expect to stay invested.
ww.The time of day that a market opens: Market opening hours are a trading schedule, whereas a time horizon is the length of your investing plan.

rw: With 40 years, a portfolio weighted toward diversified stocks has time to ride out downturns and benefit from compounding, which historically offers higher long-term growth.

ww.A single speculative bet on one company: A single speculative bet is too risky for any goal, even a long one, because one company can fail completely.
ww.Only a one-month Treasury bill held to m: A one-month Treasury bill would likely earn less than inflation over 40 years, so it is far too conservative for a long-term goal.
ww.Only cash kept hidden under a mattress a: Cash under a mattress earns nothing and loses buying power to inflation over four decades, so it is a poor choice.

rw: For a one-year goal, protecting principal matters most, so savings accounts or CDs offer safety and easy access, even though returns are modest.

ww.All of the money in cryptocurrency coins: Cryptocurrency can swing wildly in weeks, and a one-year goal cannot absorb a large drop, so it is too risky.
ww.All of the money in a single volatile te: A single volatile tech stock could fall sharply, and with only a year, there is no time to recover.
ww.All of the money in a long-term growth f: Long-term growth funds hold stocks that can fall in the short run, which is risky when you need the money in a year.

rw: A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors with money from newer investors rather than real profits, and collapses when recruits run out. Bernie Madoff ran a famous one.

ww.A savings option that banks offer to sav: Savings options offered by banks are legitimate products; a Ponzi scheme is a fraud that pays returns using money from newer investors.
ww.A bond program run by the government for: Government bond programs are legal and backed by the government; a Ponzi scheme is an illegal fraud.
ww.A legal retirement plan for workers and: Legal retirement plans such as 401(k)s are regulated; a Ponzi scheme is an illegal fraud with no real investments.

rw: Guaranteed high returns with no risk are impossible in real markets, so this is a hallmark of fraud. Higher returns always involve higher risk.

ww.A registered adviser with a public recor: A registered adviser with a public record is a sign of legitimacy, since you can check their background through regulators.
ww.Independent audited statements and recor: Independent audited statements indicate transparency and accountability, so they are a good sign, not a red flag.
ww.Clear disclosures of risks and fees to i: Honest disclosure of risks and fees is expected from legitimate investments, so it is a good sign rather than a warning.

rw: Inflation risk is the chance that rising prices erode purchasing power, so money earning less than inflation buys less over time. Cash savings are especially exposed.

ww.The risk that tax rates will rise again: Higher tax rates are a different issue, called tax risk; inflation risk is about prices rising faster than your returns.
ww.The risk that a bank closes its doors fo: A bank closing is institutional risk, which FDIC insurance covers; inflation risk concerns loss of buying power.
ww.The risk that a company fails and cannot: A company failing to repay lenders is credit or default risk, whereas inflation risk is about rising prices reducing what your money can buy.

rw: A higher interest rate, or APY, earns more interest on the same deposit, so comparing helps your savings grow faster.

ww.Lower rates always earn you more money e: Lower rates earn less, not more, so comparing rates is done to find the higher one.
ww.Rates do not affect how much you earn at: Rates directly determine your interest earnings, so claiming they have no effect is wrong.
ww.All accounts pay exactly the same rate t: Banks set different rates, so accounts differ; online banks often pay more than traditional branches.

rw: A minimum balance requirement is the lowest balance you must maintain, or you may be charged a monthly fee or lose interest. Compare accounts for low or no minimums.

ww.The most money you are allowed to keep i: The most you may keep is not a minimum; a minimum balance requirement sets the lowest amount you must maintain.
ww.The number of deposits that you must mak: The number of deposits is a transaction rule, whereas a minimum balance concerns the amount of money in the account.
ww.The interest that you must earn each mon: Interest you earn is the bank's payment to you; a minimum balance is the least amount you must keep in the account.

rw: An emergency fund covers unexpected costs like car repairs or job loss, preventing debt. Most advisers suggest building a starter fund before other goals.

ww.A luxury purchase: A luxury purchase is a want, not a priority; essential protections like an emergency fund should come first.
ww.A fancy vacation fund: A vacation fund is a nice goal, but it comes after building basic financial security.
ww.A risky investment: Risky investments should come only after you have a safety cushion, so they are not a good first goal.

rw: Withholding spreads tax payments across the year, so you do not owe a lump sum on April 15. The amount depends on income and your W-4.

ww.To keep the money as a bonus for the fir: Withholding is not a bonus for the employer; the money is sent to the government as an advance payment of your tax.
ww.To lower the worker's total income by la: Withholding does not reduce your total income by law; it is just part of your pay sent toward taxes you owe.
ww.To pay the employee in advance for futur: Withholding is a deduction from pay, not a payment to you; employees are paid after work is done.

rw: A large refund means more tax was taken out than owed, so the worker gave the government an interest-free loan. Adjusting the W-4 raises take-home pay.

ww.The worker did not earn any income last: A refund requires income and tax already withheld; a worker with no income would have no tax withheld to refund.
ww.Too little tax was withheld from paychec: Too little withholding results in owing money at tax time, not a refund, so this is the reverse situation.
ww.The employer paid the worker a surprise: A refund is not a bonus from the employer; it is the worker's own overpaid tax being returned.

rw: Self-employment tax is about 15.3 percent, covering Social Security and Medicare that employers normally split with employees. Self-employed people pay both halves.

ww.A property tax that is charged on a home: Property tax applies to real estate, whereas self-employment tax is a payroll-type tax on net earnings.
ww.A tax that applies to gifts given to emp: Gift tax applies to large gifts; self-employment tax is for those who work for themselves.
ww.A sales tax that is added to the price o: Sales tax is collected on goods sold; self-employment tax is based on a person's net earnings from self-employment.

rw: A resume is a short document summarizing your education, skills and experience to persuade employers to interview you.

ww.To list the prices of your services for: A list of service prices is a price sheet or quote, not a resume, which presents a person's qualifications.
ww.To apply for a bank loan for a home: A bank loan application is a different document that asks about income and assets, not employment qualifications.
ww.To report your income to the tax agency: Income reporting is done with tax forms like the W-2 and 1040, whereas a resume summarizes qualifications.

rw: Total compensation includes salary and benefits: Job A is $38,000 + $5,000 = $43,000, versus $38,000 for Job B, so Job A is worth more.

ww.Neither, because the benefits have no va: Benefits like health insurance have real financial value, since you would otherwise pay for them yourself.
ww.Job B, because it pays the same salary w: Job B pays the same salary but lacks benefits, so its total value is lower, not higher.
ww.They are exactly equal in total value to: The offers are not equal because Job A adds $5,000 in health coverage, giving $43,000 against $38,000.

rw: Besides pay, people are more satisfied with supportive workplaces, chances to grow, and work that matches their interests and values.

ww.The number of coworkers who happen to sh: Coworker birthdays are trivial, whereas satisfaction depends on meaningful factors like the environment and opportunities.
ww.The length of the daily commute and noth: Commute matters but is not the only factor; satisfaction also depends on environment, growth and interests.
ww.The color of the walls in the office and: Wall color is minor; satisfaction comes mainly from the work environment, growth opportunities and interest fit.

rw: A receipt is proof of purchase for returns, exchanges, warranty claims, and tax deductions or business expenses. Keep receipts for big purchases.

ww.They lower the price of the item at a la: Receipts do not change a price later; stores may offer price adjustments, but a receipt itself does not cut the price in half.
ww.They let you spend the same money a seco: Receipts cannot be used to spend money twice; they are records, not currency or credit.
ww.They are required by law for every purch: Receipts are not legally required to be filed with the state; they are kept for your own protection and records.

rw: Store cards often give an opening discount or rewards at that store but usually carry high APRs, and can only be used at that retailer or its brands.

ww.Lower interest rates than any other bank: Store cards typically have higher interest rates than bank cards, not lower, so the claim is the opposite of the truth.
ww.Free money that never has to be paid bac: Store credit is borrowed money that must be repaid, so there is no free money involved.
ww.Complete protection from fraud and ident: Store cards give limited fraud protection and no complete shield from theft; they do not prevent identity theft anywhere.

rw: Deferred interest plans may charge all back interest from the purchase date if the balance is not fully paid by the end, so shoppers should check the terms.

ww.Whether the item is also available in ot: Color options are a product feature, not a financial risk of the payment plan.
ww.Whether the logo of the store looks attr: The logo's appearance is irrelevant to the cost; the financial risk comes from the terms, fees and interest conditions.
ww.Whether the shopper has friends who also: Whether friends use the plan has nothing to do with its cost or risk; what matters are the plan's fees and conditions.
